core: What a digital footprint is: the trail of data a person creates while using the internet, spanning sites visited, messages sent, accounts opened, and information collected about them

The distinction between the ACTIVE footprint (data shared deliberately: posts, comments, reviews, uploaded photos/videos, form and sign-up entries) and the PASSIVE footprint (data collected as a by-product of use: IP address, approximate location, browsing activity, device/browser type, cookies and identifiers)

Why footprints PERSIST: deleting an original rarely removes every copy because others may screenshot, save, quote, or re-share it; search engines and web archives cache copies; platforms keep backups; even private messages can leak
The REPUTATION dimension: employers, schools, landlords, and others search people online and background checks include public online activity, so a footprint has long-term consequences
METADATA as a hidden footprint: files (especially photos) can carry date/time, device, and GPS location; the recipient of an original file can read it even without a location caption

MANAGING a footprint: searching your own name, tightening privacy settings, limiting what you share, deleting unused accounts, removing photo metadata, requesting removals, and the limited EU 'right to be forgotten' (right to erasure) with its exceptions
supporting: That reducing what you create upstream is more reliable than chasing copies downstream; the goal is deliberate curation, not total erasure
That the EU right to erasure is defined in GDPR Article 17 and is not absolute, and that comparable rights differ by jurisdiction
outOfScope: The mechanics of data collection, tracking technologies, PII, and data brokers in depth (owned by 'Privacy'); this lesson references them only to describe the passive footprint and removals
How web browsers work as applications and their private-browsing modes in depth (owned by 'Browsers')
How search engines crawl, index, and rank (owned by 'Search Engines')
Password and authentication guidance in depth (owned by 'Password Security'); mentioned only as a footprint-management aside
Individualized legal advice on GDPR or state privacy laws

claims.claim: A digital footprint is the trail of data a person creates while using the internet, including websites visited, emails sent, and information submitted or downloaded.

An active digital footprint is data created through intentional actions such as posting on social media or completing online forms, while a passive footprint is data collected without the person's deliberate action through monitoring tied to things like IP addresses, undisclosed cookies, and location tracking.

As people browse, sites can record which pages were visited, how long was spent, the searches performed, and the device and browser used; first-party tracking is by a site you visit, and third-party tracking lets another company follow you across many sites.
Online content tends to persist: information cannot be reliably erased once it has been collected or copied by multiple parties, and even private posts and direct messages can leak.
A poorly managed digital footprint carries reputational risk and can lead to problems with background checks and identity theft, because online activity is discoverable and searchable by others.
Photos and other files can carry metadata such as GPS location, and this information can expose where a photo was taken; safety guidance recommends removing metadata from photos before sharing.

Practical footprint management includes searching your own name to see what is public, reviewing and tightening privacy settings (a periodic check such as every few months), deleting old or unused accounts, and requesting removals, rather than attempting to erase yourself entirely.

The EU General Data Protection Regulation grants a 'right to erasure' (the 'right to be forgotten') that lets a data subject obtain deletion of personal data in defined situations, but the right is not absolute: Article 17(3) provides exceptions, including where processing is necessary for freedom of expression and information, compliance with a legal obligation, or the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims.

sourceRecords.title: Digital footprint (ITSAP.00.133)
sourceRecords.notes: Government of Canada guidance (February 2024). Defines a digital footprint as 'the trail of data you create while using the Internet.' Distinguishes active footprints (intentional actions like posting on social media, completing online forms, accepting cookies) from passive footprints (data collected unknowingly via monitoring tied to IP addresses, undisclosed cookies, location tracking, activity logging). Lists risks of a compromised footprint: identity theft, issues with background checks, and reputational harm. Notes metadata in photos can expose location and advises removing metadata from photos before sharing, using restrictive privacy settings, and reading privacy policies. Primary anchor for the active/passive split, reputation, and metadata claims. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: How Websites and Apps Collect and Use Your Information
sourceRecords.notes: FTC consumer article. Explains that sites can record the pages you visited, how long you spent, what you searched for, and the device and browser you used, and can show personalized ads based on browsing history or location. Defines first-party tracking (by a site you visit) and third-party tracking (another company tracking you across most sites you visit). Management guidance: delete cookies and clear browsing/search history, adjust browser privacy settings to block sites from seeing history or location, and notes a private browsing mode 'deletes your browsing history after you end your session, but it doesn't block websites from seeing your online activity.' Read via curl with a browser user-agent (default fetcher 403s). Supports the passive-footprint/tracking and management points. U.S. government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: How to: Manage Your Digital Footprint
sourceRecords.notes: EFF guide, licensed Creative Commons Attribution. Describes searching your name in a search engine to find publicly discoverable personal information; distinguishes information you post voluntarily (pictures, videos, reviews, forum comments, classifieds) from data aggregated passively by third parties such as data brokers that collect, repackage, and sell personal information. Emphasizes that information cannot be fully erased once collected by multiple parties and that brokers repopulate scraped records, so management is ongoing. Practical steps: audit yourself by searching your name in private browsing, secure accounts, review privacy settings, request removals from data brokers, and use search-engine 'results about you' tools. Facts synthesized in original wording; attribution recorded per CC BY.

sourceRecords.title: Tread Lightly Online: How to Check and Manage Your Digital Footprint
sourceRecords.notes: National Cybersecurity Alliance consumer article. Advises periodically searching your own name on search engines to see what is publicly visible, warns that 'even private posts and DMs can leak,' recommends reviewing and adjusting privacy settings regularly (suggesting roughly every three months), and recommends identifying and deleting old or unused accounts because fewer accounts mean a smaller footprint. Supports the persistence-of-private-content and management claims. REFERENCE_ONLY; described in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 17 - Right to erasure ('right to be forgotten')
sourceRecords.notes: GDPR Article 17 grants a data subject the right to obtain erasure of personal data 'without undue delay' on defined grounds (data no longer necessary; consent withdrawn; objection with no overriding grounds; unlawful processing; legal-obligation erasure; children's data). Article 17(3) sets exceptions where the right does not apply, including where processing is necessary for 'exercising the right of freedom of expression and information,' compliance with a legal obligation or a public-interest task, public-health reasons, archiving/research/statistical purposes, or 'the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims.' Supports the claim that the right to be forgotten exists but is not absolute. Canonical text cited to EUR-Lex; verified via the gdpr-info.eu reproduction of Article 17.
